name: UV-protective sunglasses

lead: UV-protective sunglasses have lenses that block ultraviolet radiation, usually labeled UV400 or 99 to 100 percent of UVA and UVB. They protect the thin skin around the eyes and cut squinting, which users link to crow's feet and early lines around the eyes.

Lens materials and coatings absorb UV before it reaches the eye, and frames shade the eyelids. Tint darkness does not indicate UV blocking. Published studies are mostly lab measurements of lens transmission and awareness surveys, and no trial has tested whether sunglasses reduce wrinkles. Dermatology and ophthalmology guidance recommends UV-blocking eyewear as part of sun protection.

paras: People wear them outdoors in bright light, often choosing larger or wraparound frames for more coverage, and use sunscreen on the skin they do not cover.
Poor-quality lenses can have a dark tint but little UV blocking, which dilates the pupil and can increase exposure. Sunglasses do not protect all the skin around the eyes.

chain: Fewer crow's feet, younger eye area
angle.text: UV-blocking lenses shield the delicate eye-area skin from sun and cut squinting, which users believe keeps crow's feet and early lines from forming. The UV blocking is a labelled property; the wrinkle link is user-reported.

lead: UV-protective sunglasses are tinted eyewear whose lenses absorb or block ultraviolet (UV) radiation as well as reduce visible glare. Labels commonly describe such lenses as blocking 99 to 100 percent of UVA and UVB rays, or use the term UV400, and experts cited by Wikipedia recommend lenses that block at least 99 percent of UV up to 400 nm [1][2].

In appearance-focused communities they are discussed as protection for the eyelids and the thin skin around the eyes, an area where lines and wrinkles are often said to appear early, and as a way to reduce squinting, which proponents associate with crow's feet. The Skin Cancer Foundation recommends UV-blocking sunglasses as part of general sun protection, and Wikipedia notes that oversized sunglasses cover more skin around the eye [1][2]. Sunglasses are also a long-standing style accessory, worn by film stars since the early 1920s and tied to designs such as the Aviator and Wayfarer [2].

Published studies on sunglasses are mostly laboratory measurements of lens transmission, assessments of eyewear used during UV phototherapy, and surveys of public awareness. No trial has tested whether wearing sunglasses reduces wrinkles or crow's feet in the periocular skin specifically [3][4][5].

paras: Sunglasses reduce the amount of light reaching the eye by absorbing, reflecting or filtering it. Lenses may include a UV-absorbing material or coating, independent of how dark the tint is. The Skin Cancer Foundation advises choosing sunglasses that block 99 to 100 percent of UVA and UVB and publishes a Seal of Recommendation for products [1].

Common types include polarised lenses, which reduce glare reflected from non-metallic surfaces such as water and roads, photochromic lenses, and wraparound or sport frames that cover more of the peripheral field [6][2]. Wikipedia notes that oversized sunglasses cover more skin and offer more protection from sunburn, though sunscreen should still be used [2].

Eye shading is old: Inuit snow goggles of walrus or caribou ivory with narrow slits date to at least the 13th century, and smoky quartz glasses were used in China by the 12th century, reportedly by judges to conceal expressions [2]. In the late 18th century Venetians wore tinted glasses, and around 1752 James Ayscough experimented with tinted lenses, although for vision correction rather than sun protection [2]. Jean-Marie-Théodore Fieuzal argued for UV protection with yellow-tinted glasses in the 19th century, Rodenstock may have made the first sunglasses intended to block UV in 1899, and cerium-glass Crookes lenses that blocked UV followed in 1913 [2].

Film stars popularised sunglasses in the early 1920s, Sam Foster began selling celluloid sunglasses under the Foster Grant name in Atlantic City in 1929, and in 1936 Edwin Land's Polaroid filter enabled polarised sunglasses while Bausch and Lomb introduced the aviator design [2]. Life reported in 1938 that 20 million pairs had been sold in the US in 1937 [2]. Ray-Ban Wayfarers, introduced in 1952, were worn by James Dean, Elvis Presley and the Beatles, Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis popularised oversized frames in the 1960s, and a 1982 product placement in Top Gun and Cobra was followed by a 40 percent rise in sales in 1986 [2].

The international standard ISO 12312 has three parts: general-use sunglasses (first published 2013, new edition 2022), direct-sun filters (2015) and sports sunglasses (2022) [2]. Europe's EN 1836:2005 uses categories 0 to 4 by visible-light transmission and has no UV400 rating, Australia and New Zealand use AS/NZS 1067:2003 with ratings 0 to 4, and the US ANSI Z80.3 limits UVB transmittance to 1 percent or less [2]. Labels in the market often use the informal UV400 term.

Lens materials and coatings absorb UV radiation before it reaches the eye, and the frame shades part of the eyelid and surrounding skin [1]. Wikipedia states that a dark lens without UV protection can be more harmful than no sunglasses because the pupil opens wider and admits more UV [2]. A darker tint is therefore not in itself an indicator of UV filtering.

Separately, proponents of sunglasses for skin care say that squinting contracts the muscles around the eye and, repeated over years, contributes to expression lines. Reduced squinting in bright light is proposed as an indirect wrinkle-prevention benefit. This mechanism has not been tested in a published trial.

UV exposure is associated with photokeratitis, cataracts, pterygium and eye cancer, according to Wikipedia, and high-energy visible light has been linked to age-related macular degeneration [2]. The Skin Cancer Foundation states that basal cell carcinoma makes up about 90 percent of eyelid skin cancers, squamous cell carcinoma an estimated 5 percent or more and melanoma 1 to 2 percent, that most occur on the lower lid, and that at least 10 percent of cataract cases are attributable to UV exposure [1]. The Foundation also says a hat with a brim of at least three inches can block up to half of the UV that reaches the eyes and eyelids [1]. Cumulative UV exposure is also stressed in public-awareness research [5].
No clinical trial in the reviewed literature has tested sunglasses against a control for wrinkle prevention or periocular skin ageing.

Related laboratory and applied research exists. A 1995 study in the International Journal of Dermatology measured 34 pairs of sunglasses to judge their suitability for blocking UVA in patients undergoing PUVA treatment, who are advised to protect their eyes on treatment days; patients had found many dedicated UVA-blocking shields cosmetically unacceptable [3]. A 2007 study tested 16 branded and unbranded UV-protective sunglasses sold in India inside UV phototherapy chambers to compare their protective properties [4]. A 2022 cross-sectional survey in Jordan assessed awareness and knowledge of UV effects on the eye and of protective practices, and noted that UV exposure is cumulative and has serious ocular complications [5]. These studies concern eye protection and product performance rather than facial skin outcomes.

Sunglasses do not cover all periocular skin, and sun-protection guidance generally continues to list sunscreen, hats and shade as additional measures [1][2]. Lens quality varies: the studies of eyewear in phototherapy settings found differences in measured UV protection between products, including between branded and unbranded pairs [3][4]. Wikipedia also notes that polarised lenses are considered undesirable for pilots, because aircraft windscreens and some cockpit displays interact with polarised light [2].

In sun-care and style discussions, sunglasses are treated as a low-cost accessory that does two jobs: shading the eye area and framing the face. Proponents describe them as complementary to sunscreen rather than a replacement for it, and appearance writers also discuss frame shape in relation to face shape.

Consumer guidance such as that from the Skin Cancer Foundation addresses how to select sunglasses, including looking for stated UV protection (99 to 100 percent of UVA and UVB, or UV400) [1]. Tint darkness is not an indicator of UV blocking [2]. Wraparound or larger frames cover more skin [2].
